Member would agree that it would be in the interests of all who are opposed to that absolutely offensive regime and all who are offended by the attacks authorized by the Government of South Africa to find some way, working with India, Australia, and our other friends in the Commonwealth and elsewhere, to be able together to accomplish more than one nation acting alone might accomplish.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-92, an Act to regulate interests in petroleum in relation to frontier lands, to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act and to repeal the Canada Oil and Gas Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

When the House adjourned at one o'clock there were four minutes remaining in the question and comment period with regard to the speech of the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow). There being no questions or comments, debate.

Mr. Speaker, in participating in the debate on Bill C-92 I want to say to the House that the particular difficulty I have with this Bill is similar to the difficulties, which I now see in retrospect, with what they sometimes call the wisdom of hindsight, I had with the preceding legislation, namely, the Canada Oil and Gas Act, which was promulgated in March, 1982, and which this Bill seeks to amend. In other words, the problem I see with this Bill in the one particular aspect I am going to address, was also the problem that existed in the previous Bill, which we are now amending.
Both of these measures, one passed by a Liberal Government, and this one seeking to be passed by a Conservative Government, fail, in my view, to comprehend what is involved in the unresolved settlement of aboriginal claims north of 60. That is the problem I see with the Bill, and it is on that subject alone I wish to direct my remarks.
Gurston Dacks of the University of Alberta has stated, and I agree fully with him, the following:
The Government of Canada has historically viewed the north as a colony, and the basic thrust of its northern policy has been that the north must serve the strategic and economic needs of southern Canada.
Professor Dacks has described the native claims settlement process north of 60 as being glacial-an interesting description. He goes on to tell us what he means. He writes the following:
-it advances very slowly and, like the glaciers, will leave a profound social, economic and political mark on the north for generations to come. Until these claims are settled, the non-renewable resource industries of the north, most notably the oil and gas industry, will face native opposition to their proposed projects.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Mines who spoke first on this Bill, the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), said during the course of his speech that "as a Government we are deeply concerned with the fair and equitable treatment of Canadians from all regions and from all
May 20, 1986

walks of life". I have no reason at all to doubt the sincerity of the Hon. Member when he spoke those words. He does believe them. He is an honourable man, principled and upright in every respect. I have to point out to the House that nowhere in the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary in introducing Bill C-92 did he give even passing lip service to the concerns of northern native peoples, the Indian or the Dene, the Inuit and the Metis.
He said in his speech that there is concern for all Canadians in all regions, and yet he neglected any reference to these important people north of 60. They have to be mentioned whenever we talk about gas and oil development, whenever we talk about development of the non-renewable resources north of 60.
This legislation, Bill C-92, proceeds almost as if these people did not exist. Of course, as I started out by saying, the previous Bill this one will replace did exactly the same thing. In that regard, and in my own defence, I only want to point out that the Liberal Government's Canada Oil and Gas Act was promulgated in March of 1982. The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government did not report to Parliament until November of 1983. During the period of time that Members of Parliament for all political parties were working on that report of the Special Committee a great deal was learned by those Members. There was a good deal of sensitization to the reality of the rights and claims of aboriginal peoples in Canada.
I came to believe that, following the tabling of that report, those Members of Parliament, and I believe a growing number of other Members of Parliament, will never again have exactly the same perspective on public policy issues that in any way at all touch upon the rights and the prerogatives of native people.
It was for this reason that I was surprised that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of State for Mines, who gave the opening speech in this debate, did not put something into his speech with respect to aboriginal peoples and their rights. I say that because we were privileged to have him serve on various occasions on that Special Committee, and his contribution was in no way small.
Talking about that report of the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government, making it apropos to C-92, let me just quote one small section. On page 111 it says the following:
The resolution of land and rights disputes in the territories is an opportunity and obligation for the present generation to be generous and honest and to ensure that the indigenous people of the north are the primary beneficiaries of development there, with a fair share of resources now and in the future.
That is from the special committee's report.
I return now to the speech by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary who pointed out to the House that the Canadian Petroleum Resources Act, which will replace the Canada Oil and Gas Act, will have a simplified and fair set of rules designed to encourage exploration success in Canada's frontier regions. He said these rights will guide Governments and the petroleum industry to the exploration and development of
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
Canada's frontier and offshore resources. Then the Parliamentary Secretary told the House that the competitive bidding system will ensure maximum return. That is what he said, maximum return to Canadians as resource owners.
With great respect, I must remind the Parliamentary Secretary, and also the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), that the question of ownership of resources north of 60 is an unsettled matter. It is part of and central to the settlement of aboriginal claims.
In his speech, the Parliamentry Secretary told us that Bill C-92 respects the rights of companies, regardless of their nationality. However, nowhere did he say that it respects the rights of aboriginal peoples, those who claim right and title to those lands north of 60 that have never been surrendered. There is no document available anywhere in the archives that shows that an act of surrender took place. Aboriginal rights in that part of Canada have never been extinguished. If we now take the enlightened approach that is available to us, we will no longer hear about the extinguishment of the rights of aboriginal people since we recognize that their rights have now been enshrined in the Constitution of Canada.
However, when I listened to the Parliamentary Secretary's speech, it just seemed to confirm for me the assertion of Professor Dacks who said that from the federal point of view:
The North must serve the strategic and the economic needs of southern Canada. Northern megaprojects create southern jobs, investment opportunities, markets for Canadian manufacturers, much-needed tax and royalty revenues-
To quote the Parliamentary Secretary, this Bill is designed "to enhance the profitability of companies operating in the high cost and high risk frontier regions". I take strong exception to the Parliamentary Secretary's view that Bill C-92 introduces a balanced framework for the development of Canada's frontier lands. He pointed out in his speech that it is fair to provincial and territorial Governments and to all Canadians as resource owners. He said that the Bill is not only market responsive, it is internationally competitive and sensitive to commercial concerns of companies operating in the high risk frontier regions of the country. This may or may not be true. Those are very difficult and complex questions, most of which I will have to leave to our able energy critic, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan). The Parliamentary Secretary and the Government for whom he spoke failed to comprehend the central issue of aboriginal rights in relation to Bill C-92. In my opinion, this casts very serious doubts on the validity of the legislation we are debating today.
Let me move away from the Parliamentary Secretary's speech and turn to the Bill itself, and the Minister's statement and accompanying documents of October 30 last year, to discover whether what the Parliamentary Secretary neglected to say is mentioned anywhere at all. It is mentioned, but only parenthetically. It is in no way central to the principle of this Bill. Clause 3 states:

May 20, 1986
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
Nothing in this Act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this Act.
If we were to interpret Clause 3 of the Bill in the broadest possible sense, in an all encompassing historical, constitutional and legal way, most of Bill C-92 would be null and void. The Government is legislating for oil and gas companies to develop these non-renewable resources on aboriginal lands where claims have not yet been settled. We call these lands frontier lands or Canada Lands, simply because it serves our own purpose.
Of course, we are told in the accompanying document entitled Canada's Energy Frontiers: A Framework for Investment and Jobs that Clause 3 is to be interpreted only in a very narrow way to cover one agreement that we now have in the Northwest Territories, the Committee for Original People's Entitlement, or so-called COPE agreement. That document says:
An agreement with the Committee for Original People's Entitlement (COPE) has already been concluded and enshrined in legislation. Nothing in this policy statement or proposed legislation will alter that provision of that agreement and its implementing legislation.
We are pleased with that and did not expect otherwise. Clause 3 is in Bill C-92 for no other reason than that it is a very narrow recognition clause.
To be fair to the Minister, there is some other reference and recognition of aboriginal rights in the statement to which I just referred. Let me draw those to the attention of the House. The document says:
The North is different from other frontier regions in fundamental ways. The prospective oil and gas areas are not just offshore. They are also on land, close to northern communities and within the traditional hunting and trapping areas of people with unresolved aboriginal claims.
One can see that we are making progress but only a little at a time. The document goes on to say:
Because of the complexity and far-reaching consequences of unresolved aboriginal claims, aboriginal groups must have the opportunity to participate in-discussions to ensure their rights and interests are protected.
The document which accompanied the announcement of the new frontier energy policy indicated that the frontier energy policy has been discussed with northern native groups. That statement caught my attention immediately, and when the Parliamentary Secretary spoke I waited for some information about the conclusions of those discussions. However, there was no mention of it at all.
Quite apart from other relevant issues related to energy policy, such as Canadianization, security of supply and fairness, Bill C-92 gives me grave concern because it makes no provision for the active participation of aboriginal peoples in the decision making process related to the development of nonrenewable resources north of 60. It really ignores, almost completely, the impact of aboriginal rights now recognized within the Constitution of Canada. I believe that Bill C-92 underlines the fact that these constitutional rights that aboriginal peoples now possess are no more than paper rights at the moment. The Constitution is a beautiful and impressive
document which talks about aboriginal rights. But I want to know when we will yank those rights off the paper and put them into the real world in which people live. We have not even begun to do that.
A very distinguished Canadian lawyer who has worked effectively in the field of native claims made this observation:
The issues are such that they can only really be resolved to the satisfaction of all through a negotiated fair settlement which requires a political and legislative approach and solution.
That statement, I believe, draws all of us in the House into the process.
There have been positive results throughout this process. The Minister of Indian Affairs asked for a task force to review the comprehensive claims policy since the old one was out of date, inadequate and unacceptable. Although it is not yet the policy of the Government, there is a report known as the Coolican report which is very important to legislation such as Bill C-92 and the process in which we are all involved in some way. The report states:
Aboriginal groups should be entitled to negotiate decision-making participation in the management and use of land and resources within their traditional areas. The decision-making structures in which they participate should have responsibilities that go beyond a merely advisory role.
It is vital that aboriginal groups be able to negotiate decision-making powers and to explore with governments the most appropriate means of sharing responsibility.
I would like to refer to the resource revenue sharing recommendation in the Coolican report. It states:
Economic participation by aboriginals in resource development could take a variety of forms. ... such participation may result from aboriginal ownership of subsurface resources in certain areas. Even where aboriginals do not own the resources, however, there are other mechanisms that could facilitate their participation in the economic benefits of resource development. Such mechanisms could include a share of royalties derived through the Crown, and a share of other revenue sources such as licence, bidding, and annual fees.
None of that is in Bill C-92.
I will conclude by saying that the Minister, in introducing this new frontier energy policy, espoused for the House a principle I like very much and that is the principle of shared management. However, what the Minister meant by "shared management" was the Government of Canada, the oil and gas industry, the provinces and the territorial Governments. I have to remind her and the Parliamentary Secretary who introduced Bill C-92, that north of 60, sharing means involving another important group, perhaps the most important people who live there, namely, the aboriginal people. Their rights and their claims are paramount. If any of us are in any doubt about that, the Constitution of Canada makes it abundantly clear.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to engage in debate on Bill C-92, the Canada Petroleum Resources Act. It is a very important piece of legislation designed to meet a number of objectives. It is important that we appreciate what the
May 20, 1986

consequences may be for Canada, particularly in the circumstances of great change in the energy industry we are experiencing in 1986. It is also important for us to look critically at this Bill, because this is the larger part of the Conservative program to destroy the national energy policy of the early 1980s and to redesign the rules and structure for the petroleum industry in Canada which the Conservatives regard, of course, as having been so destroyed by the NEP. This is a program which is designed to re-establish the kinds of principles the Government says should prevail in the petroleum industry.
The petroleum industry is of enormous importance to us in Canada. There are a number of objectives to be achieved and we want to be sure that Bill C-92 will in fact provide for those various necessities. I think it is particularly opportune to be debating the Bill now in the middle of May, 1986, because circumstances in the petroleum industry have changed so greatly that we can already assess the validity of these decisions and the viability of the structure the Government is establishing. We have a means of questioning the advisability of this particular approach to the petroleum industry. The fact that we can do so in debate on second reading is very useful. It allows us to examine these matters quite early in the history of this Bill. If the Government were to come to the conclusion that the energy regime which it has put forward is unwise, here is the opportunity to go back to the drawing board and come up with better rules.
In expanding on this subject I would like to recognize clearly and explicitly the needs that face Canada at the beginning of this decade, and to consider the ways in which the Liberal regime was designed to deal with these necessities and whether this replacement for the Liberal program will do the job successfully.
We must remind ourselves that the National Energy Program was put forward in highly unusual circumstances which were novel at the beginning of the 1980s, although certain achievements by the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries had intensified the abnormal situation which had prevailed since the early 1970s. We must appreciate the success of OPEC in driving up the price of crude oil, and with it natural gas, and the success of OPEC in forcing consumers around the globe to pay far more for petroleum.
We must also appreciate the consequences in at least a couple of directions. The first one was obvious, and that was the unprecedented transfer of wealth from the consumers to the producers. It opened possibilities for economic development in countries which had only dreamed of such possibilities before. It has had enormous consequences with consumers trying to maintain themselves by borrowing money and ending up as the debtors of world banking institutions in a way which threatens the economic stability of the entire western world.
Another consequence of the great increase in petroleum prices was to open new possibilities for exploration as well as to open the potential, at least, for alternatives to displace petroleum as a fuel in those instances where that could be
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
done. I have in mind the possibility that these high prices would lead to exploration in the areas where exploration needed to be carried out, given the declining reserves and the fall off in exploration in the older areas, and I am thinking of Canada and the United States in particular, the continental reserves. To compensate for those declining reserves through the 1970s was one of the challenges we faced. The Governments worried about and grappled with the need to ensure that we would have security of supply in the future.
What is surely significant is that the regime which prevailed until the beginning of this decade, in which tax incentives were the main encouragement to exploration, had not had much success. Even when petroleum prices rose, as they did quite substantially in the 1970s-although relatively speaking they skyrocketed at the very end of the decade-there had not been very much success in the offshore areas or the so-called "Canada Lands" north of 60. That limited success is reason for asking ourselves whether a return to the regime of that era will be successful in our time. It is reason for asking at the outset whether security of supply, which is quite fundamental to our industrial economies and to the transportation systems on which we as consumers depend, will be provided for.
The Government did not see security of supply as the only objective on which the National Energy Program was based, and I recognize that as well. There were other objectives. One was to ensure an increasing ownership of petroleum and also to ensure that the people of Canada could, through tax schemes, share in some of the windfall gains which producers were trying to achieve, not because their costs of production were high but because they had succeeded through Cartel organizations in driving the price of petroleum so high. It is in considering these various objectives that the National Energy Program becomes such a complex matter with which to deal. On the one hand, trying to achieve security of supply led the Government to advance subsidies and grants in the amount of millions of dollars toward exploration in the areas where there had not been much accomplished before 1980. On the other hand, it appeared clear to the Government in those days that there were possibilities for compensating these expenditures by means of a tax regime through the petroleum and gas revenue tax that brought in large amounts of money, the kind of windfall gains the OPEC organization made possible even for countries that were not in any way members of the OPEC organization.
The combination of the PGRT with Petroleum Incentives Program and other provisions designed to achieve 50 per cent Canadian ownership along with the recognition that the people of Canada were in one way or another paying most of the costs of this exploration and the provision of 25 per cent of discoveries going to the Crown made up the provisions of the National Energy Program which Conservative Members in opposition found so objectionable. Why they found them so objectionable is a consideration on which it is worth spending a moment.

May 20, 1986
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
Conservative supporters in the petroleum industry, particularly those from the large multinational corporations controlled outside of Canada, found receptive ears in Conservative circles. They found ready listeners to the argument that this kind of energy regime was completely unfair. One need only read the statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) when she presented this scheme to appreciate the kind of moral fervour the Minister built up over what the multinationals saw as the unfairness of this particular system.
These corporate spokesmen persuaded the Conservative Party to destroy most of the National Energy Program while leading Conservative Members to think that thanks to prevailing high petroleum prices, exploration would go on with encouragement from tax incentives to the extent they were needed. The oil companies would be allowed to take most of the windfall gains, even if it took a few years to move to that regime, and then Conservative Members would hope quite devoutly that these oil companies would do the exploration required to ensure security of supply.
That is the reason the events of 1986 posed such a great challenge to the Government's legislation. It is the reason for the crisis that OPEC itself now faces as petroleum prices fall to levels lower than most people had believed or lower than, at certain moments at least, most consumers had hoped. It is there that one sees a crisis for the energy program of the Conservative Government and right there where Bill C-92 comes immediately into question. It is worth reading some of the statements made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on Wednesday, October 30, when she proudly presented to the House of Commons the agenda for the destruction of the National Energy Program. At that time, she said the following:
Mr. Speaker, the reaction to these initiatives has been very encouraging.
Oil exploration in western Canada is now higher than at any time in our history!
Overall oil and gas investment intentions are up by about two billion dollars; more than a 25 per cent increase over last year.
This investment is providing energy security and economic benefits-jobs- right across Canada.
As well, deregulated oil markets are creating opportunities for both producers and consumers.
It does not take very much knowledge of the present circumstances to know that oil exploration in western Canada is not higher than at any time in our history. The oil and gas investment intentions of about $2 billion have shrunk considerably in the present circumstances. The investment that was providing energy security, economic benefits and jobs right across Canada is very close to lying in shambles. The Accords so proudly put forward by the Government as being its own political and moral solution to the situation created by the National Energy Program are not being realized.
Oil companies which had great hopes of profiting from the windfall gains that OPEC had made possible in the past are now laying people off, cutting back on drilling plans and
returning to the circumstances of the 1960s and the 1970s. They are putting in fundamental question the possibilities of oil self-sufficiency for the people of Canada. There lies the fundamental weakness of this scheme.
Conservative Members thought that they could return to the days before 1980. Their friends in the oil companies were happy about that because it was going to give them a larger share of the very large pie which OPEC created while the Government gave up its share. Now, thanks to what has happened in the international petroleum industry, the whole scheme is in question.
If we were to have Bill C-92 before us in the House and in committee for several months longer, we would have more time to consider carefully the system with which the Government has come up and to discover exactly how far it will fall short as a basis for maintaining oil security, quite aside from concerns about Canadian ownership and other concerns of the petroleum industry. It seems to me that that is the largest difficulty that faces the Government. By its mistakes, that difficulty can be imposed on the Canadian people.
There are questions to be raised, and if I am raising spectres, I hope on behalf of the Canadian people that they are not justified. However, these days there is no assurance that this particular triumph of ideology in the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources will not leave us begging, freezing or standing still in the future. Then Canadians will look back on the Government they elected in 1984 and will curse it for what it did to Canadian people.
Let me deal with several other important aspects of the Bill. I have already explored the dependence on market forces which is central to the Government's action. I would say it is profoundly hypocritical to talk about depending on market forces when the first reality of the market is the triumph of an international cartel that has been rigging prices at incredible levels. At least intellectually, we now have the satisfaction of looking at market forces and deciding if dependence on them is such a bright idea. I know that the Parliamentary Secretary is listening to this with care because he will be there along with others answering for the Government when Canadians find themselves in the cold.
Dependence on market forces then is doubtful. Among the provisions of the Bill is one for competitive bidding based on a single criterion. The Parliamentary Secretary suggested this morning that it could be possible for various items to be written in, and that there could be a recognition of the needs of aboriginal peoples north of 60 with title not yet extinguished in so many areas and with concerns about their own benefit from petroleum. The provision is there, but many of us do not trust the Government when it comes to such things. Given its surrender to petroleum companies on the fundamentals of the regime, we do not trust that the Government will do anything better there. However, I suppose that for the Government to say at the outset that it will be a single criterion, or that it might be written up so that various things are provided, is perhaps not much weaker than leaving the matter less clear
May 20, 1986

and saying that a variety of provisos or criteria will have to be confronted by the bids. All of this from one Government is neither here nor there.
I should like to refer to the matter of the sharing of the people of Canada in successful exploration. Before the National Energy Program was brought in Canadian people paid some 90 cents out of every dollar of exploration costs. This was made more explicit through the Petroleum Incentives Program which paid the money up front so that people could see the totals. The decision to move away from that kind of system to one which hides grants in tax expenditures is surely objectionable at a time when the entire tax scheme comes under more and more question. As a result of this we also lose the possibility of the people of Canada sharing by the Crown share, the 25 per cent share proviso which was part of the National Energy Program. This opened possibilities north of 60 for aboriginal peoples to take a fractional share of that in government programs and so on and so forth.
There are other weaknesses in Bill C-92, weaknesses which I think are quite fundamental as other Hon. Members have stated them. However, in my mind they do not bulk as large for the people of Canada as do fundamental questions about security of supply in this regime which I have explored primarily in my speech this afternoon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member was all over the map. He did not come right out and say-and I would like him to come out and say it-that the reason drilling and exploration were down at the present was because of the energy policies of the Government. He knows that this is not true; he knows that it is because of the low world price of energy today. He also knows that Canadian energy is very expensive. The only solution the NDP has suggested is the establishment of a floor price; in other words, to have Canadian consumers pay more for gasoline than the price at which we export the product and to allow imports to come in at a lower price. I do not think Canadian consumers would appreciate paying more for their resources than the price of those being exported. The next thing in the line would be to say that we should cut off exports. Then what would we do with 600,000 barrels per day of heavy oil which are being used in the United States for its road upgrading program? I am sure westerners would really love to hear the Hon. Member advocate that we should not export any of our oil and gas to the United States at market price but at the price Canadians are paying, at which point no one would buy.
The NDP arguments have flaws all over the place. If the Hon. Member had been honest in his speech, he would have pointed out that the low price of world energy today has a lot to do with the downturn in the industry.

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the Parliamentary Secretary making these arguments. They allow one to come to grips with the hypocrisy of
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
the Government's program and to deal with its weaknesses. Whatever criticisms he may have of my arguments, Canadians are not particularly interested in my arguments this afternoon. However, they have a crucial concern about the Government's program and whether it will work. I did not think it was necessary to say that the situation at present is so bad because of the low price of petroleum, although I said it. It has been the failure of the cartel arrangement which has cast us into this new situation.
The Government was sure that it could allow its friends in the oil companies to make billions of dollars thanks to OPEC. The Government withdrew from that area and left it to the companies. As I said before, it assumed all along that prices would remain up there somewhere and that exploration would continue. It was a matter of talking market while the industry wanted to profit from the most massive global intervention into the market that anyone has ever seen.
I should like the Parliamentary Secretary to concede that OPEC created this artificial situation with enormous economic rents to be captured. Oil companies wanted to have it all and not to allow the Government to share in it. Now that OPEC falls into difficulty, prices come down, oil rigs are left parked, and lawyers are laid off in Calgary, as one of the ultimate measures of how tragic is the situation in western Canada, the Government, perhaps to its credit, will stick rigidly to principle. It will go on talking market while we get closer to market forces prevailing. We in the New Democratic Party do not worship market forces. We think society deserves the guidance of the best minds in Government, and we do not only depend upon the market. We are looking at what might be done in the way of maintaining the industry and ensuring security of supply for the future. Rather than shooting at me on that, the Parliamentary Secretary might pay serious attention to how his government program will provide that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to get a clear indication from the Hon. Member of what is their policy. I have not heard what the NDP would do. He talks about market forces not working. Consumers in Canada are benefiting very well today from the market-place. The market-place is working. In 1985 we had more exploration than we ever had. There was more activity in the energy field than before as a result of the policies of the Government. Prices were steady. Throughout 1985 the price per barrel of oil was steady. There was no great increase or decrease throughout 1985 until the end. I say to the Hon. Member that a year and a half ago lower prices were predicted by all of us, including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) who stated before the Western Accord was signed that oil prices were on their way down.
The NDP likes to throw around the red herring that the Conservatives are the friends of the oil companies. I should like to ask the Hon. Member why Canadian companies asked us to get off their backs and out of their hair. Why did they ask for the cancellation of the National Energy Program? He thinks that only five or six oil companies asked for it. I can tell

May 20, 1986
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
him that that is not true at all. The Canadian industry-and our oil industry is now almost 50 per cent Canadian-asked the Government to get out. It was not only the big oil companies about which the Hon. Member likes to talk, the oil companies which the NDP likes to paint as the big bad bogymen in the whole scenario.

Mr. Speaker, I have several points to make. It would be useful to have these letters tabled in the House so that we might all see the extent to which companies other than the Seven Sisters, or whatever their number is these days given the changes in the oil industry, were actually desirous of that sort of change. A reason for all of those who had great ambitions was to take advantage of the situation which continued to prevail in 1985, whatever thought there might be that prices would drop a little. No one really thought they were going to drop in this disastrous way, disastrous for producers and consumers in the long run given that there would be nothing quite so happy as burning all the petroleum we had in cars and in other ways at 25 cents a gallon. We could all be overjoyed at something like that. I am grateful that the Parliamentary Secretary frowns because he realizes his argument is a stupid one to put forward.
The difficulty we face is to find out what kind of a price and what kind of a regime we need to maintain exploration and to ensure that something resembling security of supply is a reality without oil companies being able to run away with us and our wallets, allowing consumers to maintain some sort of a reasonable standard of living. Those are the concerns. How to do that is not an easy matter. I depend on our critic for energy to lead in these areas rather than spelling things out myself. I can assure the Member that we are not adverse to considering regulated prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: At what level?

That is a nice question, at what level? The Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) this morning was talking about $18 to $20 U.S. as the basic level at which the industry could operate. I do not know when we are going to see $18 to $20 U.S. again.
What do you mean? It was $17 U.S. today.

If we do not reach that level, what are we going to see? The schizophrenia in comments is lovely. Last year it was Government policy that lead to all this exploration. This year when levels fall off it is world economic forces. Politicians have a tendency to believe that good news is thanks to them and bad news is thanks to others, preferably international forces beyond the control of the Canadian people. That is the situation we are in these days, Mr. Speaker. It is no easy matter to resolve. I will leave whatever I have said about hypocrisy and other things this afternoon. We have a limited understanding about market
forces when the cartel is triumphant, but at least there is some consistency now in continuing to talk market forces while the petroleum industry gets somewhere closer to market realities in terms of 1986.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: You have no idea what realities are.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I was talking to the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) who had the good fortune to spend last weekend down south. He was telling me that the price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. is considerably lower on a proportionate basis than it is in Canada. That raises the question as to what the great market policies of the Government have produced when Canadians are paying hundreds of millions of dollars more for gasoline today than consumers in the U.S. are paying on an equivalent basis.
I have in front of me a survey of investment spending produced by the Canadian Petroleum Association. Market price is just one aspect. Another thing we could look at when we study the over-all policy of the Government is investment spending by the industry. In a recent survey, the Canadian Petroleum Association estimated upstream capital and exploration expenditures for 1986 to be 43 per cent lower than in 1985.
In 1985, the actual expenditures by the industry were $10.5 billion and the intentions for expenditure in 1986 were originally forecast to be $11.2 billion. It seems that the revised intentions forecast of expenditures is only $6 billion.
Since upstream spending was a significant portion of total business investment in 1985, the downturn will significantly impact not only on western Canada but on the economies of Ontario and Quebec.
If one wants to look at employment, public announcements to date indicate personnel reductions in operating companies of over 4,000 employees. Reductions in spending will severely impact in the drilling, service and oil field goods manufacturing which will cause additional widespread lay-offs. Statistics Canada estimates a loss of 10,000 jobs during March and April in Alberta alone. This loss was essentially related to the downturn in the oil and gas sector. Unemployment in Alberta rose to a seasonally adjusted rate of 9.7 per cent in April. The Calgary rate, I understand, was 10.9 per cent and Edmonton's was 12.5 per cent. Where are the benefits that have been produced by the Government's energy policies in Alberta?
Only 39 rigs were drilling in western Canada at the beginning of May, 23 in Alberta. There has been no recovery despite the lifting of road bans, and this low level is moving now into its fifth week, the longest sustained slump at such a low level in the past 13 years. Drilling completions for 1986 are currently estimated at less than 7,000 compared with nearly 13,000 last year.
Crown land sales, regarded as the bellwether indicator of industry health, have dropped significantly in total bonuses and prices per hectare. To the end of April Alberta land sale
May 20, 1986

receipts were down an astonishing 52 per cent to $113 million compared to $236 million in the comparable 1985 period.
What about productive capacity? Lower oil prices and the resulting decline in upstream investment, especially the reduction in exploration, will have serious consequences for Canada's future crude oil production. A recent assessment of the productive capacity by the Canadian Petroleum Association indicates that productive capacity of light crude oil would decline approximately 30 per cent to 700,000 barrels a day by 1990, and 58 per cent to 420,000 barrels a day by 1995. Lower oil prices will also affect synthetic crude projects, bitumen production and conventional heavy oil output. Any additions to productive capacity or replacement of diminished output due to natural reservoir decline is currently expected to come only from bitumen products that are already in the construction or pre-production phase. Over-all, the assessment indicates that statistical self-sufficiency could be lost by as early as 1990 and a significant supply gap would develop by 1995, which could make Canada dependent upon imported oil for some 30 per cent of requirements.
With regard to the Canadian balance of payments, I am not telling anyone anything they do not know by saying that the export of oil and gas has made a significant contribution to Canada's balance of payments, its positive merchandise trade balance over the years. The price drop which we are suffering from at the present time will significantly affect that position. Indeed, the effects are already showing up. In 1985, exports of crude oil and natural gas were valued at $9.8 billion. The changes between the exports in the first quarter of 1986 and those in the first quarter of 1985 are astonishing.

speechtext: In volume or price?
In price, Mr. Speaker. In the area of crude oil there was a drop of 28.2 per cent in the first quarter of 1986. There was a drop of 22.6 per cent in natural gas for a total drop of 25.4 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Tell us about the volume.

The Parliamentary Secretary says: "Tell us about the volume". It is, of course, the reliance on market forces and the willingness of the Government to accept the market price and all that comes with it that produces this effect on our economy. If the current price situation and marketing difficulties prevail, the 1986 exports are likely to drop below $6 billion. This, of course, is the situation of lower oil prices and how it will affect the petroleum industry in Canada. The outlook is not very encouraging.
I would also like to comment on the renewable energy industry in the country. One of the first initiatives of the new Government when it took office was to eliminate totally the energy division at the National Research Council. All research in energy in areas of wind, solar energy and biomass were cancelled. Canada had reached the point where it was
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
developing world-class technology. We were starting to export to the counties of Africa and many other world markets. One of the first things that the Government did was to cancel all research into renewable energies, which left the industry in the position of exporting a product with the possibility of no future development.
If one looks at this in the short term on the basis of the low energy prices from the end of 1984 until today, one could find it difficult to justify expenditures on renewable energy which may be much more costly in the short term. Is this the way to go about securing Canada's energy self-sufficiency for the future? Surely the Government should be preoccupied with the situation which may prevail five or ten years from now when energy prices may again be at the level which pertained at the end of the 1970s and in the early 1980s. Surely we should be concerned about the energy self-sufficiency of the country when the hydrocarbons which we are presently consuming will be exhausted.
The energy policies of the Government seem to demonstrate a concern for the short-term and neglect the long-term perspective which is essential in considering the general impact of Canada's responsibilities in the world.
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech of the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) because he has a great grasp of the scientific aspects of the renewable energy industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Be serious, Doctor.

I heard the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary earlier this afternoon. He was acting as if the Government really knew what it was doing. One need only consider the fact that there are 36 out of 480 rigs in the western sedimentary basin which are operating. The article says:
Each week, rigs are coming back in from the fields and not going back out. The banks are becoming wary about making loans. Producers are cancelling their drilling contracts. Whole floors of office towers in Calgary are emptying out.

It is not that the members aren't hearing the cries of anguish from their constituents. "Calgary is in a disastrous state", says Bobbie Sparrow, one of the city's four MPs. I have not heard what the Government is going to do as a result of that caucus meeting a month or so ago. Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to speak on Tory energy policy because it is pretty clear that the tooth fairy has landed. This is a wish list for the corporate board rooms of the big oil companies. My colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway and I sat for months with some of the same Tories here today and fought against Bill C-48 and all the Mack truck loopholes it contained. Now we find the Government side, now that it is Conservative, suddenly quiet because many of the wishes provided by the big corporations at that time we now find in Bill C-92. It calls for us to go through it with a little bit of care. I will highlight a few of the more glaring Mack truck sections, because I would not want to bore anyone who has to watch this debate or read this in the near future.
There are an awful lot of Canadians who do not know what lands are really affected. It is all of the Yukon, all of the Northwest Territories, all of the offshore up 200 miles, and all of the Arctic Archipelagos; all of those waters.
On that point I find it interesting, coming as I do from the North and travelling frequently, particularly in the Yukon, to have listened over the years to Yukon Erik and to the present sitting Tory Members in the Northwest Territories who, during the last election, were out there campaigning, and campaigning hard, saying that it is about time the Yukon got provincial status and provincial powers. They said that it is about time the Western Arctic got real powers and that they are going to fight for that in Ottawa. The Hon. Member for the Eastern Arctic said, "It is time for Nunavut. I am going to change the name to Nunavut and we are going to have real powers for the Inuit and the people who live north of sixty".
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
This certainly lays to rest the promises of those three Members coming to Ottawa to come into this Parliament and to fight for what most, if not all, northerners want, which is some sovereignty in their own area.
I can remember Tory Members in the last House talking about assisting to set up a heritage fund in relation to gas and oil and energy for the Yukon, for the Western Arctic and the Eastern Arctic to help with the Northwest Territories so they could get their own university, their own services and have their own sources of revenue. There is not even a whisper of any of that in here.
As a matter of fact, as a northerner you have to listen to this to get the drift of where this new administration is going. They define frontier lands in the following manner:
"Frontier lands" means lands that belong to Her Majesty in right of Canada, or in respect of which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources and that are situated in (a) the Yukon Territory, the Northwest Territories or Sable Island, or-
And this is where British Columbians who are listening should be interested to learn about the land grab about which the Tories stood up in this House five years ago. It was described as the greatest land grab of the century, the land grab off the B.C. coast, around the Queen Charlottes, the Dixon Entrance and the Hecate Strait, down in Queen Charlotte Sound, west coast Vancouver Island. They decried it and said it was terrible. On the East Coast it was already under way off Newfoundland, P.E.I., New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, that is all in here. This is pounding those last few nails that the oil companies wanted to see pounded in to make sure they could get whatever they wanted.
We have to look at some of the Mack truck sections of this Bill to see what is in this tooth fairy energy Bill, Bill C-92, that these great fighters for Canadian rights and northern sovereignty bring to us. My colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway raised Clause 3 on aboriginal rights, which says the following:
Nothing in this Act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this Act.
We went through the constitutional debate. We have the now Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) on the record as saying that it is likely that there is aboriginal title in British Columbia. We are in the process of negotiating the settlement of outstanding aboriginal claims in the Yukon, in the Western and in the Eastern Arctic. Nothing is happening in British Columbia, and in terms of the offshore, this Bill tries to extinguish some of those outstanding and, as yet, unnegotiated and unresolved legitimate claims to aboriginal title, particularly in terms of the offshore.
What became of this open Government that was going to negotiate, sit down with the Government of Yukon, the Government of the Northwest Territories, the aboriginal peoples north of sixty, and particularly in British Columbia, to talk about a heritage fund, to talk about participation, to talk about the process of farming in to these various developments, both onshore and offshore? There is not a peep. There have

May 20, 1986
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
been no discussions, no negotiations, and certainly nowhere in this legislation do we find anything that remotely resembles any kind of an architecture that would allow for the proper easy flow-in of those rights as they are negotiated in tandem with the introduction of this kind of legislation.
Aboriginal people in Canada should know full well that this is a shot across their bow. There is a test here by the Mulroney administration to see whether or not aboriginal peoples will sit down and quietly accept this kind of an approach by Conservatives from British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, which is completely contrary to what they have spoken about in terms of the election.
Let us take a look at these Mack truck loopholes that I have alluded to, because I look forward very much to hearing Conservative Members, particularly from B. C. and the North, explaining what these kinds of loopholes really mean. Let me refer to page 12. This is where the Government sets up a nice little regime that looks as if it were going to provide a regulatory regime that protects the public interests. It is Clause 26, subclauses (3), (4) and (5). I want to refer to subclause (4) where it says the following:
The Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing areas in respect of which the Minister may make an order pursuant to subsection (5).
We have to read subclause (5), and it says the following:
The Minister may, subject to such terms and conditions as the Minister deems appropriate, extend the term of an exploration licence in relation to any frontier lands within a prescribed area that has been renegotiated under subsection (3).
We have had to read subclause (4) to get to subclause (5). Now we have to read subclause (5) to get back to Subclause (3). Subclause (3) says the following:
Subject to subsection (5) and Section 27, the term of an exploration licence entered into or in respect of which negotiations have been completed before December 20, 1985 may be renegotiated once only for a further term not exceeding four years and thereafter the term thereof shall not be renegotiated, extended or renewed.
If you go through Subclauses (3), (4) and (5), what you find out when you read subclause (5) is that it is all politics. The tooth fairy has landed once again. Any large corporation that wants an extension of any kind can simply get it. This is what I described as setting up a regime and then designing a loophole. That is just the kind of thing the big oil companies like to have.
Let us go on to what is called the lapsing of interests in Clauses 42 and 43. This is called subsurface storage licences, which anyone who has read any evidence of the Beaufort panel or the recent B.C. offshore panel knows that this Government, and certainly the Government of British Columbia, constantly attempt to downgrade, denigrate, and do whatever else they can to destroy the very important environmental concerns that are brought forward. Let us have a look at how you get a licence for subsurface storage. Clause 43 says the following:
The Minister may, subject to any terms and conditions he considers appropriate, issue a licence for the purpose of subsurface storage of petroleum or any other substance approved by the Minister in frontier lands at depths greater than twenty metres.
It sounds innocuous enough, does it not? One of the great concerns about lifting the moratorium off the B.C. coast, and as has been demonstrated in offshore drilling elsewhere in the world, is that there is an enormous amount of waste product every day. Your average size offshore semi-submersible or jack-up rig has about 10,000 barrels a day of drilling mud and fluid, much of which is extremely contaminating to the environment and can in fact in very short order kill off not only the vital plankton and the small plants near the surface of the ocean, but also affect salmon, perhaps in British Columbia, the whale populations, marine birds and so on in the North. These are crucial questions.
Here we have a Mack truck loophole to allow companies that find that there is a particularly suitable area either onshore or offshore. It is not limited, so they can simply pump their refuse down so long as it is 20 metres or more underground or underwater. This is very interesting. I have worked on oil rigs in the Northwest Territories and northern Alberta. I know what can happen when drilling companies do not have very specific written regulatory regimes under which to work. Their purpose is to make money, and if there is nothing prohibiting them from dumping all of their detritus into the ocean, an estuary of a river or on the land, that is exactly what they will do. No one should accuse them of wrongdoing because they have not been given prescribed conditions under which they can operate. Once again, the tooth fairy has landed with another mac truck loophole.
During all the years I have been in the House, and long before I was elected, the Conservatives always argued against Governor in Council regulations. Yet Bill C-75, introduced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), has no regulations. We will only see those regulations after Parliament has passed that legislation. We are seeing the same red tape that the Tories campaigned about at each election, saying: "Vote for us and we will cut the red tape. Don't worry, we will do it for you". However, since September 4, 1984, as much if not more red tape has been created than I and I am sure most Canadians have ever seen.
It's blue.

That is right. As my colleague points out, blue ribbon is the new fantasy of the day, certainly as it pertains to Bill C-92.
Let us examine Clause 100 dealing with regulations. It states:
The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations
(a) prescribing the powers, duties and functions of the Registrar and Deputy Registrar for the purposes of this Part and the time when, and manner and circumstances in which, they are to be exercised, and providing for the designation by the Minister of any person or class of persons to exercise such powers and perform such duties and functions as may be specified in the regulations;
May 20, 1986

That long paragraph of nonsense comes from a Government that promised faithfully to get away from the gobbledegook, in terms of the Income Tax Act, new laws and how Parliament would be run, and would bring in regulations along with the Bills. Once again, however, there are no regulations in the Bill. They will be produced by bureaucrats, ferreting away in their dark corners, typing Governor in Council regulations so that the Cabinet can decide exactly what they will mean.
I am sure that British Columbians assume that they will be directly involved in the panels and boards that will be set up, particularly those concerning environmental matters. I am sure that the Indian, Inuit and Dene people north of sixty, as well as Yukoners and those who live in the Northwest Territories believe they will be involved in these panels and boards. I am sure that Canadians from Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec believe that the new Conservative Government will involve them in these issues.
However, let us look at Clauses 75 to 83 with regard to membership on the environmental studies management board. That membership is restricted to employees in the Public Service of Canada. The same bureaucrats who will be making the regulations that do not appear in Bill C-92 for our consideration will sit on the board to interpret what other studies should be funded or considered. The tooth fairy has truly landed for the oil companies. Not only do they get everything they want in Bill C-92 because the Government discarded everything they did not like in Bill C-48, but everything that the Government and the oil companies are afraid to tell the Canadian public will be produced in regulations later on. The same bureaucrats, under the same government administration and listening to the same corporate boardrooms will make the decision as to what happens. The Conservatives who campaigned on open Government are closing the doors even faster than their Liberal pals ever did on Bill C-48 and other legislation. It is enough to make one want to throw up. I suppose it is still parliamentary to use the word "crap" to describe this and, as a westerner, that is the message I will deliver far and wide.
Anyone who wants to be thoroughly nauseated should read Bill C-92. It is so full of regulatory loopholes that it would make one dizzy.
Let me move on to look at what happened with the Beaufort panel. Northerners were encouraged to participate in this hearing. They came from communities far and wide to express their concerns about the environment, land use, employment and their involvement in businesses associated with the oil patch. They were interested in getting a heritage fund and participating as provincial members in Canada's Confederation. The Conservatives, in the same fashion as the Socreds or the Liberals, set up these panels and invited people to become involved. These ordinary citizens, whether they were local dry-cleaners or trappers, used all their energy, working on their own time, to appear before the panel and make their views known. However, after all of that energy, has been expanded,
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
as happens every time, the report is published and then sealed away in a secret area in Ottawa where these kinds of studies are tabled and kept in perpetuity.
Many northerners hoped that at least some parts of the evidence brought before the Beaufort panel would ultimately find its way into legislation. However, with three Tories representing the North, there was not a peep, a word or a ray of light relating to the Yukon becoming a province, the Northwest Territories being divided into two provinces or there being sovereignty for northerners, particularly the Inuit, and Indian and Dene people.
Let us examine what happened in British Columbia. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) just tabled a report on the West Coast offshore. All Members know that Petro-Canada promptly withdrew from those hearings when it realized that the amount of accurate scientific information it had on drilling in areas such as the offshore of the West Coast was totally inadequate. However, Chevron continued to participate in the hearings and dilly-dallied along.
The information contained in Chevron's environmental assessment was preposterous. One piece of evidence that was tendered to the offshore panel comes to mind when I see the kind of jurisdictional grab that the Minister is interested in taking in this legislation. The evidence that was tendered originally to the offshore panel indicated that drilling would be safe in the Hecate Strait because it was protected from the open Pacific by the Queen Charlotte Islands. Obviously, someone took their pudgy finger and pointed at the map and saw that there were some islands and only 70 miles of water, which would make the Hecate Strait the same as a lake.
The fact is that drilling has taken place in the Hecate Strait and waves close to 100 feet high were breaking over the deck of the boat that was trying to drill at Cape St. James. There was a 20 foot chop on top of the waves that were breaking over the top of the boat. Members opposite cannot believe that but they probably believe the evidence of the oil companies that the Hecate Strait is flat, calm.
This legislation is unacceptable. The same Tories who used to accuse the Liberals of taking a grab from the public of Canada are doing the same thing, along with their friends south of the border and the oil companies in Canada.
The Conservatives said that the 25 per cent back-in was a preposterous rip-off. They should consider how almost every other state in the world protects the public interest and not always the interest of the oil companies. We should protect the public interest to make sure that all Canadians, young and old, whether from the East, the West, or the North, get a fair rate of return from an energy source that we all own.
The Conservatives seem to forget that we all own the gas and oil. Whether it is on land or offshore it belongs to all of us and we deserve a fair rate of return from it. This Bill strays very far from that, and I condemn most strongly its inability to

May 20, 1986
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
understand the importance of environmental concerns. The board will be composed of bureaucrats, all appointed from the Public Service, with perhaps a few members from the provinces. There will be no opportunity for native people to be involved, nor for environmental groups. There will be no opportunities for the fishermen of Prince Rupert. There will be no opportunity for any of those groups which have a lifelong abiding interest in what happens to the environment. If the fish go, they have no livelihood. If the kelp or the shellfish go, they have no livelihood. Entire communities can vanish, and all of the effort put into the panel hearings in British Columbia and in the Beaufort in the North has come to nil. Bill C-92 is a disaster for the average Canadian. It is a Mac truck tooth fairy dream.
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for the usual way in which he lays it out as it is.
Objective and scientific.

Objective and scientific as well. There was one small inaccuracy and that is when the Hon. Member referred to me as having raised the matter of native rights. I believe it was the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry). Apropos of that, since the Hon. Member did deal in his speech with aboriginal rights and with environmental matters in some depth-which I have not heard too many other Hon. Members do-I want to ask him about Clause 3, which states:
Nothing in this Act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this Act.
The Hon. Member might think this is a phoney question or I am trying to pull something on him, but if I was going to ask a question, it would be, who is worse as far as aboriginal people are concerned, the federal Conservative Government or Premier Bill Bennett of British Columbia? It is like choosing between being hanged and being drawn and quartered. At least Bill Bennett spells it out that he is against aboriginal rights, refuses to live up to the Constitution of Canada and will not deal fairly with native people. But it is beyond me why the Conservative Government has thrown in Clause 3. Either we are prepared to recognize aboriginal people's rights and are prepared to deal with them or we are not. This clause is like a Bill to expropriate a house. We are told that nothing in the Bill is going to affect our quiet enjoyment of the House, and then the rest of the Bill goes on to say that the House is going to be flattened and all our property is going to be taken away from us.
Could the Hon. Member who represents the Nishga's, the initiators of aboriginal rights, explain to the House and to the public why it is that this is not satisfactory? What do the aboriginal people want when they want their rights respected in a Bill which deals with resources and so much of the territory, especially in the North, to which they lay claim?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the question because it really is one of the keys to what is wrong with this legislation because of what is said in Clause 3. It basically maintains the status quo. There have been no serious negotiations with aboriginal people regarding resources in British Columbia or, to a great extent, north of 60. All Clause 3 says is that that is going to continue. One has to look at what has been going on since September 4, 1984, to get an idea of why aborigal peoples are becoming so rapidly disillusioned with the new Government. One must look at the Buffalo Jump, the 1980s Cabinet document which came to light just a year ago, which indicated the desire of the Government to move down the same road which was stopped by the famed Calder case before the Supreme Court of Canada in 1972. What happened there was that the then Liberal Government was proceeding down the road known then, and still known through the White Paper, as the "assimilation model", that was to try to get Indian, Inuit and Dene people from across Canada to move into urban centres and away from their traditional homelands where they had historically lived, not just for centuries but for thousands of years. One must put together the pieces such as the Buffalo Jump of the 1980s, the Nielsen Task Force report on funding to Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the debate going on, at least in the mind of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), on the question of extinguishment.
Rather than proceeding as is recommended in the Coolican report, the Minister and the Cabinet seem to be seized with the inability to understand why we cannot simply extinguish aboriginal title and rights. It is something that would take far longer in terms of time than I have available to explain everything which has gone on in terms of the Calder case and the initiatives taken by groups such as the Nishga for more than a century. They have travelled here to this Parliament and to Great Britain and have met with every panel and every forum. They have taken advantage of every legal opportunity, but they are still stonewalled.
Bill C-92 is a challenge to the living title of aboriginal people, particularly from where I come, and I am referring to the Haidas, their claim to title and their sea claims around the Queen Charlotte islands, which is jeopardized by this kind of legislation, which is neither constitutionally nor legally sound for the reasons outlined in this House the debate on the Constitution, and the inclusion therein of the existence and affirmation of aboriginal rights which flow from the title. In terms of the coast and the A-B line debate, there is something very fuzzy in the Bill which I am sure the U.S. State Department is examining now that it has appointed Mr. Derwinski to look at the 141st Meridian in the Beaufort where it leaves lands end between Alaska and Yukon and goes north, the A-B line at the southern extremity of the Alaska Panhandle.
This Bill is very fuzzy. It claims jurisdiction to the Continental Shelf but does not delineate under what precise legal principles we are going to extend our boundary from Cape Muzon to the 200-mile limit nor in terms of the Strait of Juan
May 20, 1986

de Fuca boundary, the 141st Meridian, the eastern perimeters of the Arctic Archipelago and our offshore on the East Coast. This is a Bill which is fraught with difficulties and, as my colleague has said, it shows a lack of understanding of the issues which aboriginal people want to see dealt with in fairness. They want to have negotiations on the sharing of resources because access, control and ownership of resources is what gives us sovereignty, and that is what the aboriginal people are asking for.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a short question. I know the Hon. Member is interested in the job side of the whole energy legislation. The Government when elected was determined to create some 100,000 to 300,000 jobs in the energy field, so we were really shocked on March 21 to read in The Globe and Mail that Imperial Oil was set to slash 1,800 jobs because of oil prices and chemical glut cited. I was especially concerned because it was just about this time that Algoma Steel started laying off some 300 or 400 workers at its tube division at Sault Ste. Marie, which is really dependent on the oil industry because the tubes it produces are used in oil and gas exploration and drilling.
There were some comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary, that the worst was over, that oil prices had rallied from $11 to about $17 over the weekend. Yet in The Globe and Mail today, exactly two months after those first indications of lay-offs by Imperial Oil, there is a report that Occidental Petroleum in Los Angeles is cutting 2,000 employees from its payroll in order to reduce its 1986 spending budget. The same article in this morning's Globe and Mail business page indicates that Exxon Corporation of New York, the largest oil company in the United States, shocked Wall Street recently when it offered a voluntary resignation program to 40,000 of its employees, about 27 per cent of its world-wide staff or 59 per cent of its domestic staff.
I would be interested in hearing the comments of the Hon. Member from British Columbia. I know that oil and gas exploration is important there and in the North as well. The Western Accord and the frontier legislation brought in by the Government is really not adequate to deal with the kind of oil price drop which we have seen. One short paragraph about violent fluctuations in oil prices just does not seem to be adequate, and certainly those articles about Imperial Oil and Exxon indicate that there are a lot more people in this industry to be laid off. Certainly that will be harmful not only in B.C. but in the North as well because of the lack of government policy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the question. I want to make it clear from the outset that what is happening in the oil patch cannot be placed entirely on the back of the new Government. At the same time, the Parliamentary Secretary cannot pop up every time someone speaks to say that the new drilling opportunities that occurred last year were all due to the new Government's
Canada Petroleum Resources Act
policies. He cannot have it both ways. If he is going to take credit, he has to carry some blame.
I think the point made by the Hon. Member who just asked the question is something at which the Government ought to take a close look. Lay-offs in big companies in the oil and gas industry and the chemical industry are tough. In those cases, hundreds and thousands are laid off. However, when a small Canadian producer in northeastern British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan lays off half a dozen employees, the whole company is gone. Then those interests are very quickly picked up by the big players who still have the internal ability to create capital and pick up those operations.
Rather than addressing the serious problems facing all of the companies in the industry, and particularly the Canadian ones, the Government is dreaming and spinning its wheels. It is bringing in tooth-fairy legislation designed for the boardrooms when it should be doing something not only to help consumers but to help small Canadian drillers and operators in the oil patch.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-92. First of all, I must say that, once again, the little guy is going to be the loser.
Mr. Speaker, if we look carefully at Bill C-92, we could say this is a typically Tory piece of legislation, because here again, big business-the big oil companies-is going to reap the benefits.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to regulate interests in petroleum in relation to frontier lands, and "frontier lands" mean lands that belong to Her Majesty in right of Canada, or in respect of which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources and that are situated in the Yukon Territory, the Northwest Territories or Sable Island, or any other off-shore areas.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk to you about a trip I made a week ago, when I spent a week or so in Canada's North, and I am referring to the Arctic. I must say that this trip made me discover this vast country and its people, and I was very impressed to see the kind of facilities that exist in the North. However, what really struck me during my trip is that in every community there was this almost exclusive dependence on oil for electric power and for heating purposes. In those communities, the people have yet to benefit from the drop in world oil prices, for the simple reason that their oil is shipped in bulk at least one season in advance, and there have been no shipments yet for this year.
Well, they are certainly in for a surprise, because even if they hear about falling oil prices and the fact that there has been a substantial drop, they will soon realize that they will not be able to take advantage of these lower prices. They will certainly have a few questions to ask the Government, such as why they can't benefit from this drop in the price of energy.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that they need this energy daily and they have to pay for the energy they use.
In the course of our hearings, we met many residents of those vast territories who had some very interesting stories to tell. At one hearing in one particular town, where a Minister of the Government of the Northwest Territories testified-the purpose of our hearings was to examine deregulation of transportation in Canada's North-one question led to another and the subject of energy came up. At this point, a Government Member who was indulging in a bit of partisanship, which I think we can tolerate from time to time, Mr. Speaker-in fact, I do this myself occasionally-this Member asked the Minister whether the National Energy Program had in any way contributed to the development of the Northwest Territories. The Member, who was expecting a negative reply, was of course astonished when the Minister answered that if it had not been for the NEP, our northern regions would certainly not have experienced all the development that has taken place since the program came into effect. This, of course, led the Member who asked the question in the first place to change the subject-
And talk about the weather.

At the outset I want to say that it became evident that for the third year in some areas a drought was inevitable.
